How green are electric cars?

By: Neil Shaw | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Globally, and that includes South Africa, we are on the cusp of an electric car revolution. But just how green are electric cars?

Unique Selling Point:
Looking at a fresh angle about electric cars: the mineral resources needed to produce these massive car batteries.

Summary:
1.Presenter charges up an EV (electric vehicle) in Jo’burg. Explains that the owner uses home solar to recharge; that SA EV sector is nascent but big growth inevitable; questions how green they are; presenter drives off 2. Portugal lithium mining to commence. Lithium is a crucial ingredient in the very large batteries that EVs use. Speak to local who doesn’t want his area destroyed by mining. 3. ROR Mining company 4. Presenter in EV car runs through some EV negatives: expensive (thus far/in SA), recharge on dirty coal power in SA, dirty mining and battery production 5. With graphics show how a US government model indicates 130,000 kms needed for an EV’s carbon footprint to become green in a country utilising coal power such as SA. 6. Presenter arrives at a Jo’burg mine dump, references lasting legacy here, speaks on skype to Amnesty International about human rights issues around cobalt mining in DR Congo -- cobalt another key ingredient in EV batteries. + other environmental/human rights global mining issues 7. The other perspective, introduction: Auk Hoekstra who specialises in studying models comparing EV and internal combustion vehicles: His view on erroneous modeling, EV footprints are shrinking by the day. 8. Presenter in her/his EV arrives at Jo’burg location to interview energy expert Clyde Collinson, who advises the government: This is a disruption technology, by 2030 50% of cars in SA will be EVs, that SA is on the cusp of a renewables revolution (based on economics alone), plugging into renewable power dramatically alters/improves EV footprint… 9. But what about all that dirty mining? Well, battery technology is improving and will use less and less minerals. 10. Presenter arrives at a car battery recycling centre. 80% of EV batteries in Australia are being recycled for home power storage. Recycling EV batteries is going to become a massive sector globally, meaning less mining needed 11. Return the EV to its owner. Final word on “renewables revolution”

One day shooting in Portugal
One day in Jo'burg

Script:


Instead of going to school or playing with their friends, these Congolese children are mining cobalt, with their bare hands… they’re in one of the only spots on Earth cobalt can be found - a key ingredient in the global transition to green energy, powering the new generation of electric cars. 

In South Africa, this electric vehicle market is still small, with only 92 new electric cars sold in 2020.  

Good morning! Claire! A lot of people think it is quite complicated -- how do you charge an electric vehicle? It’s very simple really, it’s exactly like plugging in a kettle!

Daniel Limpitlaw is part of the small community of Johannesburg electric vehicle owners. He recharges using his home’s solar power system. 
   
What’s been happening with solar in the last five years is that the price of panels has been coming down at an almost exponential rate, so it’s becoming more and more affordable and we are going to reach the point that this becomes the more affordable option rather than the less affordable one. 

The consensus is that renewable energy is the way to go, to lower harmful carbon dioxide emissions… to halt changing weather patterns and extreme weather events world-wide. 

LINK  When the national electric grid becomes solar powered like Daniel’s set up here, rather than coal powered, then electric vehicle’s carbon footprint will drop dramatically. 

But for now an electric vehicle’s carbon footprint depends on whether it’s charged using renewable energy - like solar - or a CO2-emitting coal power source…and by the mining that takes place for its components.
    
In Covas do Barroso in the north of Portugal, residents are protesting plans for a new lithium mine.

Lithium is a key component in electric car batteries. 

I watched our producers’ earlier interview with Aida Fernandes, a cattle farmer near one of the proposed sites.

We feel sad, concerned, angry, because no one asked us if we want this project.   They want to make a big mine near the village, destroy the river, use all the water and destroy all the mountains.  If this happens, it is the end of the local people, the local community, the fields, the communal land.

The multinational Savannah Resources is behind these plans.

“From the project, there’ll be something of the order of 20 million Euros at least from taxes… so you’re looking at 250 million Euros over the life of the project…  in terms of jobs we’ll be looking at employing around about 215 people… we’ll have zero negative impact on agriculture for example…   

Aida Fernandes is not reassured by the company’s promises.

The compensation that the Company speaks about, the benefits… for us that live here, there will be no benefits. On the contrary, we will only have losses.  We will lose our land as it is a vast area that they would like to use. The majority of the people live from agriculture and by losing the land they will have to stop doing what they always did.  

The Portuguese lithium mines are among many planned across Europe. 

Lithium demand is expected to grow by 42 times over the next two decades. Other key minerals in the car  production process, like copper, nickel and cobalt have also become highly sought after.  

Children in the Democratic Republic of Congo mine for cobalt that powers up your mobile phones, computers, and electric cars. 

Mark Dummett from Amnesty International has visited the DRC’s artisanal cobalt mines repeatedly. Our producer had interviewed him earlier. 

Because this artisanal mining is unregulated no one’s got a very strong idea of exactly how many people are involved let alone how many children but it’s estimated to be in the tens of thousands in that one region… it’s driven by poverty, it’s driven by the need to eat that day…no one in their right mind would want a child as young as seven to be in these mines. The dust is potentially toxic, the work is back-breaking, they’re exposed to all kinds of risks. But at the same time we have to recognise that it is a lifeline for them. It’s how they survive, it’s how their families survive. It’s a really really complicated issue  and no easy solutions.

South Africa’s fortunes were built on minerals so it’s no secret that there is a price to pay.
LINK   We in Johannesburg know what the lasting legacy of gold mining is: acid mine drainage, and health issues for the communities living near these mine dumps.   

Clyde Mallinson is a geologist by training, and an energy analyst who advises Public Works and Infrastructure Minister Patricia de Lille. 

By 2030, the South African government wants to have wind and solar power accounting for 33% of the overall energy mix. For Clyde that’s wholly inadequate.  

He says critiques of the renewable energy transition are just a distraction - the last gasp attack of the fossil fuel industry.

Some people say electric vehicles are not really clean technology if they require six times the amount of minerals inputs as a conventional car. What do you think about that statement?

First of all, It’s completely wrong. Most of the mineral inputs are of the actual car, and an electric car has the same amount of steel and aluminium as a non electric car…. The battery does have a lot of mineral input in it that a conventional car does not have, but it’s not excessive. 

If you think of the coal mining, and oil and gas mining, and the impacts that had, you only have to look at places like the Niger delta, or gulf of Mexico to understand the quantity of coal mine is orders of magnitude greater than the mining that will need to take place for lithium and nickel and other battery elements, so it’s a red herring. 

What about the overall carbon footprint of an electric vehicle -- mining, transport of raw materials, factories where the batteries are made, and of course the power source to recharge? 

LINK   In a comparison between the lifecycle carbon footprint of electric vehicles and traditional internal combustion engines, the US government’s Argonne National Laboratory, came up with some interesting results. 

A Reuters analysis of the Argonne model shows that in coal-powered countries like South Africa you need to travel 126,000 kilometers in an electric car before becoming the greener vehicle than a conventional car. 

But Clyde doesn’t buy these lifecycle comparison models.
They misrepresent how much CO2 goes into the battery in the first place, they misrepresent how often the battery has to be replaced, they assume the CO2 from the grid will stay as bad as it is at the moment. 
For Aida Fernandes and her community in northern Portugal, exactly how green electric vehicles are is besides the point. They resist new mining in the name of the green revolution. 
And the child cobalt miners of the DRC should be getting an education, not working in danger. 
Amnesty International has been campaigning with other NGOs, civil society groups in Congo, and around the world to pressure those companies at the end of the supply chain such as Apple, and Tesla and Renault and Peugeot and Microsoft and Samsung and these companies which use the batteries to use their leverage over these other players in the supply chain, the middlemen and these companies that buy the minerals, to try and clean up ….. their supply chains, source from responsible miners”
Mining components in electric cars will pose environmental problems until batteries with fewer or no minerals go mainstream.
In the meantime recycling is taking off - which means the precious raw materials like lithium and cobalt inside the electric car battery, can be re-used.
Daniel Limpitlaw’s i3 that I borrowed is powered by the sun, and that alone reduces his car’s carbon footprint dramatically. 
That’s the unfortunate thing about South Africa at the moment. We are one of the most coal intensive countries in the world, and the whole point about moving to electric cars is we need to do it in parallel with a migration to green electricity….As we migrate to renewables, which is going to happen in about the next decade, the uptake of renewable energy in the country will match the uptake of electric vehicles. 
What people will realise is that these vehicles are so much more efficient, they’re so much cheaper to run, and when the capital costs go down, when the huge import duties and tariffs are removed, these are going to be the more affordable way to travel.   
Recycling might lessen the mining impact on the environment, but what is for sure is that an electric car plugged into a renewable energy source is a positive step in the fight against climate change.

The other perspective, introduction: Auk Hoekstra who specialises in studying models comparing EV and internal combustion vehicles: His view on erroneous modeling, EV footprints are shrinking by the day. 8. Presenter in her/his EV arrives at Jo’burg location to interview energy expert Clyde Collinson, who advises the government: This is a disruption technology, by 2030 50% of cars in SA will be EVs, that SA is on the cusp of a renewables revolution (based on economics alone), plugging into renewable power dramatically alters/improves EV footprint… 9. But what about all that dirty mining? Well, battery technology is improving and will use less and less minerals. 10. Presenter arrives at a car battery recycling centre. 80% of EV batteries in Australia are being recycled for home power storage. Recycling EV batteries is going to become a massive sector globally, meaning less mining needed 11. Return the EV to its owner. Final word on “renewables revolution”
